$comment: SPEC §34.6 — the ONE voice/call WebSocket wire protocol, for voice notes and live calls, on WS /call/session and the chat socket. Binary frames = 16kHz mono PCM chunks with an 8-byte header (4-byte monotonic seq + 4-byte flags). Text frames = JSON control events {type, seq, ts, payload} with this CLOSED type set. Server acks control events by seq. Heartbeat every 10s; server reaps at 30s silence. Reconnect within 5 min resumes via session token, else handoff.to_text fires with full context. The AsyncAPI document is generated from this package.

fields.name: type
fields.description: One of the closed event type set

fields.name: seq
fields.description: Monotonic sequence number; server acks by seq

fields.name: ack
fields.description: SPEC §34.6: 'server acks control events by seq'. There is no ack MEMBER to carry that — the set is closed at fifteen — so the acknowledgement rides on the event the server sends in reply, naming the client seq it answers. Null on client frames and on anything the server sends unprompted.

fields.name: payload
fields.description: Event-type-specific payload. Typed below for the members the TEXT chat uses; the voice members stay untyped until M9 builds them.

$text_chat_mapping.$comment: SPEC §34.6 is ONE protocol for voice notes, live calls AND the chat socket, and its type set is closed at fifteen. A text conversation therefore has to be said in members that already exist — which it can, because a typed message is the same event a spoken one produces after STT: a finalised caption. Written down here so both services read one description rather than two implementations.

client_to_server.session.start: ticket + conversation_id + locale; the ticket is minted by POST /v1/chat/session over the cookie-authenticated origin
client_to_server.captions.final: the user's finalised turn. In a call, STT finalises it; in text, the keyboard does. `quoted_message_id` carries §25.4's swipe-to-reply INTO the pipeline, not merely into the drawing.
client_to_server.vad.state: M9 — brackets a held recording (§25.4's hold-to-record / tap-lock). `speech_start` opens the window binary frames are admissible in; `speech_end` closes it and asks for a transcript; `cancelled` is §28.3's cancel-slide and discards without transcribing or storing.

server_to_client.session.ready: resume token + window; the socket is live
server_to_client.presence.state: driven by the pipeline's real §9 stage transitions. Where the pipeline reports nothing, this reports nothing — a typing indicator that keeps animating through a stalled turn is the fake online-status §25.4 already refuses, one layer down.
server_to_client.captions.partial: M9 — an interim transcript of the USER's own speech, and only ever theirs (see $never_emitted_for_tara). Advisory: the bubble may show it while STT settles, and `captions.final` replaces it.
server_to_client.captions.final: the whole validated turn (ChatTurn) in Tara's direction. In the user's direction M9 adds the finalised TRANSCRIPT of a voice note, carrying the stored asset id so the bubble can play the original. The ONLY member that ever carries Tara's words.
server_to_client.tts.start: M9 — Tara's reply is a voice note (§25.4's voice-adoption engine). Carries the synthesised asset id, duration and format. It is emitted AFTER her `captions.final`, never before: the audio is rendered from validated text, so the text exists first by construction.
server_to_client.tts.chunk_meta: M9 — metering only (§13: shapes, not content). Bytes and sequence for the client's buffer; carries no transcript, because the transcript already crossed on captions.final.
server_to_client.tts.end: M9 — synthesis complete; total duration for the bubble's scrubber.
server_to_client.handoff.to_text: the resume window closed; the thread continues over POST /v1/chat/turn with full context

$text_chat_mapping.$never_emitted_for_tara: captions.partial. A partial caption is pre-validation text, and §9 puts grounding, language-quality and safety-post AFTER generation. Streaming tokens would race past all three, so the socket is built to never hold them: it receives a finished TurnResult and has nothing else to send. That is the fabrication gate, and it is structural rather than remembered. M9 gives the member a payload for the FIRST time and does not weaken this: `PartialCaptionPayload.role` is the constant `user`, so an interim caption of the USER's own speech is expressible and one of Tara's is not. The rule stopped depending on nobody writing the frame.
$text_chat_mapping.$heartbeat: The transport's own ping/pong, every 10s — which is why the closed set has no heartbeat member. Reap at 30s of pong silence (§29.2).
$text_chat_mapping.$m10_is_the_same_protocol: M9-P10b's live call adds NO member. It was always going to be the test of whether §34.6 is one protocol or three wearing one name, and the answer is that the call is said in the fifteen that already exist — the last two payload shapes land here and the set does not move. Where the call differs from the chat is WHO opens a bracket: §25.4's note is bracketed by a finger, so the client mints the `client_message_id` before the first PCM byte; §25.3's call is bracketed by SERVER-SIDE VAD (that is what 'barge-in = just speak' means), so the SERVER mints it and sends the opening `vad.state` down. The field keeps its name because it keeps its job — it is still the one id the partial caption, the final transcript, the turn and the synthesised audio all hang off — and renaming it would have split one shape into two for a difference in who speaks first.
$text_chat_mapping.$binary: M9 answered the §33.1 storage question, so binary is accepted on the chat socket — but only INSIDE a bracket. A frame is admissible between a `vad.state: speech_start` and its `speech_end`/`cancelled`, and nowhere else; outside one it is still SYS_VALIDATION. That is narrower than 'accepted' on purpose: the bracket is what binds a run of PCM to a client_message_id, a locale and a consent posture, and PCM arriving with none of those attached is audio nobody can account for. The 4-byte header seq is checked for monotonicity — a gap fails the note rather than silently concatenating across the hole, because a note missing its middle transcribes into a sentence the user never said.

$call_mapping.$comment: SPEC §25.3's live call, in the same fifteen members. Written down beside the text-chat mapping so `services/realtime` and `apps/web` read ONE description of the call rather than two implementations of it — the same reason the chat mapping is here.

client_to_server.session.start: ticket + conversation_id + locale, exactly as the chat sends it. The ticket is minted by POST /v1/call/session, which is also where the §33.5 flag, CC-010's locale gate and the §7.3 entitlement snapshot are evaluated — a call that must not happen is refused before a socket exists.
client_to_server.session.end: the user pressed end (§25.3's red control). Metering stops here.
client_to_server.$binary: 16 kHz mono PCM, continuously, for as long as the microphone is live. A call has no hold-to-record bracket — §25.3's mute is client-hard, so silence on the wire is what a muted user sounds like.

server_to_client.vad.state: §25.3's server-side VAD, and the M9-P10b sense the member was widened for. `speech_start` opens an utterance and carries the SERVER-minted client_message_id; `speech_end` closes it. There is no `cancelled` in a call — nothing was held, so there is nothing to slide away from.
server_to_client.barge_in: the user spoke while Tara was speaking. The server has already stopped synthesising; this tells the client to drop what it has buffered and not to expect a `tts.end` for that utterance.
server_to_client.captions.partial: §25.3's live captions, of the USER's own speech only — `role` is still the constant `user`, and that is what makes captions live without racing §9's validators.
server_to_client.captions.final: the user's finalised utterance in their direction, and the whole validated ChatTurn in Tara's. Unchanged from the chat, which is the point.
server_to_client.presence.state: §25.3's call states are driven from the same §9 stage transitions the chat uses.
server_to_client.tts.start / tts.chunk_meta / tts.end: her streamed reply. `tts.chunk_meta` is finally emitted here — a note is synthesised whole and has no chunks, and a fabricated one would have made the metering look live; a call really does stream.
server_to_client.handoff.to_text: §25.3's degrade ladder and §32.9's exhaustion path, both landing in the same place: the thread continues in messages with the transcript intact.
server_to_client.resume.offer: §32.11 — a network recovery inside five minutes offers the call back rather than resuming it silently. Metering restarts only if the user accepts.

$call_mapping.$never_stored: Call audio is NEVER stored (§13, §33.1, §6.4's voice_sessions and call_sessions validators). Nothing on this socket writes bytes anywhere: the PCM is relayed to the recogniser and dropped, and the synthesised audio is streamed and dropped. The transcript is stored, because the transcript is the conversation.
$call_mapping.$one_utterance_in_flight: §7.3: 'one in-flight utterance max'. A second question arriving while the first is still being answered is not interleaved — the barge-in cancels the first reply and the second utterance becomes the turn.

SessionStartPayload.$comment: Client → server. The ticket is single-use and 60-second; §34.5's session cookies are httpOnly and first-party, and a WebSocket handshake to another origin does not carry them.

SessionReadyPayload.$comment: Server → client. `resume_token` is what a reconnect inside `resume_window_s` presents (§32.11).

UserTurnPayload.$comment: Client → server on `captions.final` when typed; server → client on the same member when the turn was SPOKEN and STT has finalised it. One shape for both because §34.6's whole premise is that a typed message and a transcribed one are the same event — the difference is which of the three §33.1 fields below are populated, not which member carries it. On a typed message they are `not_applicable` / `text_only` / null, which is exactly what the store already writes.

PartialCaptionPayload.$comment: Server → client, on `captions.partial`. `role` is the CONSTANT "user" and not a ChatRole, which is the whole point of the shape: §9 runs grounding, language-quality and safety-post after generation, so a partial caption of TARA's words would be pre-validation text racing three validators to the screen. Through M8 that was guaranteed by nobody writing the frame. Now the frame exists, for the user's own speech, and the guarantee is that there is no value of `role` here that could carry hers.

VadStatePayload.$comment: Client → server, on `vad.state`. Brackets a held recording. `client_message_id` is minted before the first PCM byte leaves, so every binary frame in the bracket already belongs to a bubble the thread is drawing — the transcript lands in a message that exists rather than appearing from nowhere when STT returns.

TtsStartPayload.$comment:
Server → client, on `tts.start`. §25.4: 'Tara's replies arrive as voice-note bubbles rendered from her TTS with transcript toggle'. Emitted after her `captions.final`, so the transcript the toggle shows is on screen before any audio plays — and is the same validated text the audio was rendered from, not a second generation.

`tts_audio_asset_id` became OPTIONAL in M9-P10b, and the null is load-bearing rather than lax. A voice NOTE is synthesised whole and stored, so it has an asset and a bubble that can replay it. A live CALL is streamed and its audio is never stored at all (§13, §33.1) — so there is no asset, and there is nothing to replay. Null is the type saying exactly that. Carrying an invented id would have promised a playback control over audio that does not exist anywhere.

`holding` marks §25.3's holding phrase — the line she speaks when §9 has out-run HOLDING_PHRASE_AFTER_MS. It is her voice but it is NOT her answer, and that difference is load-bearing on three separate paths (see the field).

fields.name: holding
fields.description:
§25.3's holding phrase rather than her answer. True when this stream is the short line she speaks because §9 has been thinking longer than HOLDING_PHRASE_AFTER_MS — she has not answered yet.

Three things downstream are wrong without it, and none of them announces itself: the screen returns to `listening` on `tts.end` and shows a mic-live indicator inviting the user to speak into a turn still in flight (which §7.3 then refuses); §33.5's `first_audio_seconds` times the PHRASE instead of the answer, turning a 5.8s reply into a 1.8s one and making the cheapest thing to fake the measure the gate reads; and the caption strip treats filler as the reply.

Adding a FIELD is not adding a member — §34.6's closed set is fifteen types and stays fifteen. It defaults to false, so every producer that predates it is unchanged and the voice-note path never sets it.

TtsChunkMetaPayload.$comment: Server → client, on `tts.chunk_meta`. §13 — shapes, never content. There is deliberately no text field: the words already crossed on `captions.final`, and a second copy travelling beside the audio is a second thing to keep in step with the validators.

TtsEndPayload.$comment:
Server → client, on `tts.end`. Total duration for the bubble's scrubber, and the signal that no further chunk meta is coming.

`holding` repeats `tts.start`'s flag so each event is self-describing. The client could infer it by remembering the start, but then the meaning of an `end` would depend on a `start` it might not have seen — and the branch it drives is whether the screen goes back to `thinking` or to `listening`, which is the difference between showing a mic-live indicator over a live turn and not.

fields.name: holding
fields.description: The stream that just ended was §25.3's holding phrase, so she has NOT answered yet — the screen returns to `thinking`, not `listening`.

BargeInPayload.$comment:
Server → client (§25.3, §7.3). Typed in M9-P10b because M9-P10b is the first milestone that emits it — the rule this package keeps, and the reason it stayed untyped through M9.

**It replaces `tts.end`, it does not precede it.** `tts.end` carries the total duration for the bubble's scrubber; an utterance that was cut has no total duration that was ever true, and sending one would put a scrubber on audio the user interrupted. So a synthesis stream ends in exactly one of two members and a client can rely on that.

`cancelled_after_chunk_seq` is the last `tts.chunk_meta.seq` the server sent before it stopped. The client needs it because it is buffering ahead of playback: without it, dropping 'the rest' is a guess about what the server had already put on the wire, and audio kept playing after the interruption is exactly the thing §25.3's barge-in exists to prevent.

EntitlementWarningPayload.$comment:
Server → client (§7.3, §32.9). §32.9: warnings at 5 and 2 minutes, in-locale, in Tara's voice, ONCE EACH — the once-each is enforced by the session, not by the client ignoring repeats.

`minutes_left` is the threshold that fired, not a live countdown: a per-second remaining-minutes feed would be §29.2's countdown, which this product does not build. `minutes_quota` is null for the unlimited fair-use tiers, which is also what makes the §25.3 plan chip render '⏳ unlimited' rather than a number.

`message_key` and not a sentence: §2.4 puts every user-facing string in the catalogs, and a sentence on the wire is a sentence no §14 reviewer saw.

TaraTurnPayload.$comment: Server → client, on `captions.final`. Carries the whole validated turn and nothing else — there is no field here for text that has not been through §9's validators.

PresenceStatePayload.$comment: Server → client. The client switches on `state` alone. `stage` is §9's pipeline step, carried for traces and analytics — a shape, not content (§13) — and deliberately not something the UI branches on: the presence state is the designed vocabulary (§4.3) and the stage list is an implementation detail that may grow.

HandoffToTextPayload.$comment: Server → client. `reason` is why the socket gave up, so the thread can say something true rather than 'something went wrong'.

ResumeOfferPayload.$comment: Server → client (§32.11). `pending_turn` is the turn that COMPLETED while the socket was down — buffered rather than re-run, because re-running a turn charges a user twice for one question.
